title: Lesson 35: The annual AI roadmap against your org's capability
description: Grounded in Lesson 35 of the AI Adoption series: why capability rather than ambition constrains the year, the difference between strategy, plan and roadmap, the five capabilities every AI initiative consumes, change capacity versus change disruption, the four roadmap lanes including an explicit won't-do list, sequencing by dependency, and kill criteria written at approval.

questions.question: Lesson 35 gives a rule for using the 0 to 3 capability score. A use case needs skills at level 2 and the team is at level 1. What does the lesson say you must do?
options: Approve the use case anyway and let the team learn on the job, since real usage builds skills fastest
Record the gap as a prerequisite in the build lane with an owner and a date, and move the use case to won't do if no one owns that prerequisite
Lower the required score to level 1 so the use case qualifies this year
Reclassify the use case from the prove lane to the run lane
questions.explanation: Lesson 35 states that every roadmap item must name the capability it consumes and who supplies it. If an item needs skills at 2 and the team is at 1, the item has a prerequisite, and the prerequisite goes into the build lane with a date. If the prerequisite has no owner, the item is a wish and belongs in the won't do lane.

questions.question: In the worked example, Owen finds that claims operations is mid-migration to a new policy administration platform, scored as a 3 on the disruption scale, through the second quarter. How does that change his roadmap, and why?
options: He drops the claims use case for the whole year because the team is too busy to be trusted with anything new
He keeps the claims pilot in the first quarter but reduces its pilot group from 60 to 40 adjusters

Claims gets no new AI work until the third quarter, because committed changes consume the same change capacity the AI program needs, and the AI roadmap is planned against remaining capacity rather than total capacity
He adds a communication campaign so the claims team understands why both changes matter
questions.explanation: Lesson 35 sets a quarterly ceiling per team and says the AI roadmap is planned against remaining capacity, not total capacity. The migration already consumes the claims team's allowance for two quarters, so its AI work waits until the third quarter even though its business case is the strongest. The lesson also says the fix for saturation is sequencing, not more communication.

questions.question: Lesson 35 requires kill criteria to be written at approval rather than after a pilot disappoints. What is the stated reason this matters?
options: It moves the emotional weight of the decision from the person who championed the idea to a number agreed in advance, so stopping becomes a decision rather than an argument
It guarantees the pilot will succeed, because everyone knows the threshold from the start
It removes the need for a named decision maker, since the numbers decide on their own
It lets the program skip the business case, because the thresholds replace the financial analysis
questions.explanation: Lesson 35 describes kill criteria as a metric, a threshold, and a date written at approval, and says their purpose is to make stopping a decision rather than an argument. The specific mechanism it names is that the weight moves from the champion to a number agreed in advance, which is why the criteria survive contact with a sponsor who is fond of the project. The lesson still names the person making the decision and still requires a business case and a maximum loss sentence for commitments.
